summary: In Dhul Hijjah of 10 AH, the Prophet ﷺ performed his only and final Hajj with approximately 100,000 companions. At the plain of Arafah, he delivered the Farewell Sermon — a comprehensive address enshrining the rights of people, the sanctity of life and property, the equality of humanity, and the completion of the religion. He asked if he had conveyed the message, and the crowd answered yes.
narrative:
The Prophet ﷺ had performed Umrah multiple times but had not performed Hajj since the Hijrah. In Dhul Qadah of 10 AH he announced his intention to make Hajj, and Muslims from across Arabia and beyond gathered to accompany him. The estimates in the sources range widely — Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari record figures of approximately 90,000 to over 100,000 companions making the journey together, though this is likely symbolic of an enormous and unprecedented gathering.

The Prophet ﷺ entered ihram at Dhul Hulayfah and made his way to Makkah, performing tawaf, sa'y, and the full rites of Hajj in the manner now preserved as the Sunnah. His detailed performance of every act of Hajj on this journey became the authoritative model for all future generations, as he instructed: 'Take from me your rites of Hajj.' The hadith recording this is preserved in Sahih Muslim.

On the ninth of Dhul Hijjah — the Day of Arafah, the culmination of Hajj — the Prophet ﷺ stood on his camel at the plain of Arafah and delivered what is known as the Khutbah al-Wada' — the Farewell Sermon. It was delivered in sections, with Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf relaying his words to the vast crowd gathered below.

Ibn Hisham, al-Tabari, and Ibn Kathir all preserve the substance of the sermon. Its key declarations included: the sanctity of every Muslim's life, property, and honour is inviolable, 'like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours'; the abolition of all pre-Islamic blood-debts and usurious interest, beginning with those of his own family; the rights of women — the reminder that they are a trust in men's hands, to be treated with kindness; the equality of all people: 'O people, your Lord is one and your father is one. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab nor a non-Arab over an Arab; nor is a white person superior to a dark person, nor a dark person to a white person, except by taqwa (piety).'

The Prophet ﷺ asked repeatedly during the sermon: 'Have I conveyed the message?' Each time the crowd answered 'Yes.' He then said: 'O Allah, be witness.' He instructed those present to convey his words to those absent, 'for perhaps many of those to whom it is conveyed will understand it better than those who heard it directly.'

During the days of Hajj, on the day of Arafah, the final Quranic revelation on the completion of the religion was sent down. Allah revealed in Surah al-Ma'idah (5:3): 'This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion.' Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ wept when this verse was revealed, and when asked why, he said: 'Nothing comes after perfection except diminishment.' He intuited that the completion of the mission signalled the approaching end of the Prophet's ﷺ time among them.

On the way back through the valley of Khumm Ghadir, the Prophet ﷺ stopped and delivered an address in which he took the hand of Ali ibn Abi Talib ؓ and said: 'Whoever's mawla I am, Ali is his mawla.' This statement, recorded across many chains, carries significant weight in Islamic history and became a point of divergence in later sectarian interpretation. Classical Sunni scholars (Ibn Kathir, Ibn Hajar, al-Nawawi) interpret the Prophet's ﷺ use of 'mawla' here as an affirmation of love and brotherhood, not a designation of political leadership — a position supported by the absence of any explicit bay'ah command and the subsequent events at Saqifah. The Prophet ﷺ also reminded the community that he was leaving behind two weighty things — the Quran and his family (Ahl al-Bayt) — and called the companions to hold to them.

The Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah after Hajj. He would live only a few more months.
